compoundNote: L-tryptophan is the essential amino acid precursor of serotonin and (via serotonin) melatonin; it also feeds the kynurenine pathway. It is distinct from 5-HTP (5-hydroxytryptophan), whose trials are not evidence for tryptophan, and from tryptophan-rich foods or protein hydrolysates/alpha-lactalbumin, which also contain competing amino acids. Positive human sleep and mood findings come mostly from gram-level doses (1-3 g/day); the trials found for this page used 1-5 g/day, and a meta-analysis found larger sleep effects at >=1 g/day than at <1 g/day. Trials in this snapshot are small and short, many are laboratory emotional-processing studies, and effects often depend on genotype or baseline state. The Performance Lab Sleep serving (200 mg) is below every dose of the trials that could be read. All pubmedUrl status values are 203 because NCBI served a bot-challenge page to curl; see statusNote.

studies.title: The impact of tryptophan supplementation on sleep quality: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression
studies.population: 18 articles collected; 4 analysed quantitatively (adults, tryptophan supplementation vs control)
studies.outcome: Sleep quality components (wake after sleep onset and others)
studies.result: Wake after sleep onset shortened (-81.03 min per g, P=0.017; SMD -1.08, 95% CI -1.89 to -0.28); >=1 g/day gave a shorter wake after sleep onset than <1 g/day (28.91 vs 56.55 min; P=0.001). No effect on the other sleep components. Only 4 trials were pooled, so the estimate is fragile.

verdicts.reason: A 2022 meta-analysis (only 4 trials pooled) found shorter wake after sleep onset, larger at >=1 g/day, with no effect on other sleep components. Individual trials: pharmaceutical-grade tryptophan improved insomnia in a 49-person 3-week trial (dose not verified); 3 g/day for 7 days improved sleep only in a genotype x neuroticism subgroup. Small, short, subgroup-dependent.
verdicts.population: adults with insomnia or sleep complaints, and stress-vulnerable adults

verdicts.outcome: Sleep quality, doses <1 g/day (such as 200 mg)
verdicts.reason: The meta-analysis separated <1 g/day and >=1 g/day and found a larger effect at >=1 g/day; no placebo-controlled trial of 200 mg tryptophan alone was identified in this search. The only blend trial (n=16, 3 days) gave no tryptophan dose in its abstract and cannot isolate tryptophan. Sub-gram evidence is therefore essentially absent.

A 2021 systematic review of 11 RCTs found 4 with significant mood differences (suggested range 0.14-3 g/day) and no effect on aggression. Laboratory trials at 3 g/day show a positive emotional-processing bias in women only, while a dose-escalation trial up to 5 g/day found no change in POMS mood scores. A 1 g/day trial found a genotype-dependent mood effect. Inconsistent across designs and outcomes.

verdicts.outcome: Mood / depression, clinical or at-risk populations
verdicts.reason: The Cochrane review (2002, 2 trials, 64 patients, tryptophan and 5-HTP pooled) found better-than-placebo effects but of insufficient quality to be conclusive. At-risk groups show small or mixed effects: mood improved but quarrelsome behaviour rose in people with a family history of depression; a 1-week multi-ingredient trial in subclinical depression showed improvement in a severe subgroup, and placebo improved CES-D equally. Not a substitute for treatment.
verdicts.population: people with depression, subclinical depression or family history

verdicts.reason: No placebo-controlled trial showing cognitive benefit from tryptophan supplementation in healthy adults was found. A narrative review says tryptophan loading consistently impairs psychomotor and reaction-time performance (mild sedation), consistent with slower Stroop responses after 30 mg/kg in an 8-person fMRI crossover; a 44-person study found a specific change in negative-feedback sensitivity but no effect on reversal learning. Memory gains are reported only in clinical or sub-clinical groups per the review.

doseAssessment.trialRange: Trials that could be read used 1 g/day (1 g tid = 3 g/day in the emotional-processing and family-history trials; 3.0 g/day for 7 days in the sleep-genotype trial; 1 g/day in the genotype-mood trial), up to 5 g/day for 21 days in the safety trial, and 30 mg/kg acute in an fMRI study. Reviews state 0.14-3 g/day for mood (2021 systematic review) and that sleep effects are larger at >=1 g/day than <1 g/day (2022 meta-analysis). Doses were not verified for the pharmaceutical-grade insomnia trial, the blend trial or the fibromyalgia combination trial.
doseAssessment.suggestedText: Performance Lab Sleep supplies 200 mg L-tryptophan per serving (per the label supplied). That is below the 1-3 g/day used in the sleep and mood trials found and below the >=1 g/day threshold at which the sleep meta-analysis found its larger effect; the broad 0.14-3 g/day mood range in one review technically includes 200 mg, but the individual trials that could be read were at 1 g/day or more, and no placebo-controlled trial of 200 mg tryptophan alone was found. Treat 200 mg as a low, unproven dose that adds to the other ingredients rather than a trial-supported effective dose. Low dose also lowers, but does not remove, the interaction concerns below.

safetySignals.signal: Eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS): the 1989 epidemic was traced to tryptophan from a single manufacturer (98% of Oregon cases vs 30-48% of controls took that product), pointing to a contaminant or production alteration rather than tryptophan itself.
safetySignals.title: Eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome associated with exposure to tryptophan from a single manufacturer

safetySignals.signal: In a South Carolina tryptophan-exposed cohort, mortality was 19% in definite EMS over follow-up (more than 3x the general population) and survivors reported lasting symptoms; no delayed-onset EMS was found in users who were not ill in 1989.
safetySignals.title: The natural history of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome in a tryptophan-exposed cohort in South Carolina

safetySignals.signal: A new L-tryptophan-associated EMS case was reported in 2011; the abstract says no cases had been described since the FDA ban on tryptophan sales was lifted in 2005 until this one. EMS is rare and linked to contaminated production, so product purity and a reputable manufacturer matter.
safetySignals.title: Post-epidemic eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome associated with L-tryptophan

safetySignals.signal: A 2023 review concludes the impurities suspected in tryptophan-associated EMS have no clear, convincing causal proof; authors are employed by an amino-acid manufacturer (CJ CheilJedang).
safetySignals.title: Safety concerns regarding impurities in L-Tryptophan associated with eosinophilia myalgia syndrome

safetySignals.signal: Serotonin syndrome risk with serotonergic drugs: a case report of serotonin syndrome after tranylcypromine (an MAOI) plus clomipramine plus L-tryptophan (PubMed record has no abstract; title only).
safetySignals.title: Serotonin Syndrome Masquerading as Status Epilepticus following Ingestion of Tranylcypromine and Clomipramine and L-Tryptophan: A Case Report

safetySignals.signal: Case report of serotonin syndrome from linezolid plus tryptophan plus metoclopramide (Spanish-language record, no abstract; title only).
safetySignals.title: [Serotonin syndrome due to interaction between linezolid, tryptophan, and metoclopramide]

safetySignals.signal: Review: severe serotonin syndrome is usually precipitated by starting two or more serotonergic drugs, and MAO inhibitors combined with serotonergic agents are especially dangerous and can be fatal. This is the general mechanism behind tryptophan-MAOI/SSRI cautions.
safetySignals.title: Serotonin Syndrome: Pathophysiology, Clinical Features, Management, and Potential Future Directions

safetySignals.signal: Dose-escalation safety: up to 5.0 g/day for 21 days caused no adverse effects on biomarkers, body weight or POMS mood in 17 healthy women.
safetySignals.title: Supplementing healthy women with up to 5.0 g/d of L-tryptophan has no adverse effects

gaps: No placebo-controlled trial of 200 mg (or any <1 g/day) L-tryptophan alone for sleep, mood or cognition was found. The only evidence for sub-gram doses is the meta-analysis comparison (PMID 33942088), which pooled few trials.
Hudson 2005 (PMID 16053244): dose, effect sizes and funding are not in the abstract and the full text is paywalled, so the strongest-looking insomnia trial could not be dose-checked.
The only blend trial resembling the Performance Lab Sleep mix (PMID 36094342) has no component doses in its abstract, n=16, 3 days, and includes glycine and L-theanine but not lemon balm.

No trial combining tryptophan with magnesium, tart cherry and lemon balm was found; the only magnesium+tryptophan items are a fibromyalgia combination RCT (PMID 40151031) and a diet study (PMID 32224987, not read).
No independent healthy-adult RCT of cognition benefit exists in what was found; the evidence points to no gain and possible slowing.

Interaction evidence is case reports and mechanism reviews; no trial quantifies serotonin-syndrome risk of low-dose tryptophan with SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, linezolid, triptans or tramadol (searches run, nothing found). Two case-report records have no abstract (PMIDs 36561019, 19828401), so doses in those cases were not verified.
Pregnancy, breastfeeding, liver and kidney disease, and surgery: no human safety source was searched or found in this pass.
Funding not verified for most trials (abstract-only reads); sponsor status of PMIDs 16053244, 25644221, 25733537, 33986613, 31902864, 36094342 and 40151031 is unknown.
